file_summaries.title: Common Errors in CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Type Errors: Missing annotations, wrong types
Memory Errors: Out of bounds, alignment issues
Synchronization Errors: Missing barriers, race conditions
Compilation Errors: Syntax, imports, JIT issues
code_snippets:
@cute.kernel
def with_sync():
    smem = cute.make_smem_tensor(cute.make_shape(256), cutlass.Float32)
    tid = cute.arch.thread_idx()[0]
    smem[tid] = tid
    cute.arch.syncthreads()
    value = smem[(tid + 1) % 256]
constraints: All kernel parameters must have type annotations
Use CuTe types, not Python types in kernels
Maximum threads per block is 1024 on most GPUs
Block size should be multiple of warp size (32) for efficiency
Ensure all threads in block reach syncthreads()
file_summaries.compressed_summary: This guide addresses common errors in CuTe DSL kernel development, focusing on type, memory, launch, synchronization, and compilation errors. Type errors often arise from missing annotations or using incorrect types, which can be resolved by ensuring all kernel parameters are properly annotated with CuTe types. Memory errors, such as out-of-bounds access, require diligent bounds checking and correct shared memory allocation. Launch configuration errors typically involve exceeding the maximum threads per block or using non-optimal block sizes, which should be corrected by adhering to GPU constraints. Synchronization errors, including missing barriers and race conditions, necessitate proper use of syncthreads() to ensure all threads reach synchronization points. Compilation errors often stem from syntax issues or unsupported Python constructs in JIT compilation, which can be mitigated by using only supported constructs and verifying function availability. To prevent these errors, developers should validate kernel inputs, ensure tensors are on the correct device, and follow a comprehensive debugging checklist. By addressing these common pitfalls, developers can enhance the reliability and performance of their CuTe DSL kernels.

file_summaries.title: Debugging Techniques for CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Start with the simplest possible test to isolate bugs effectively.
Use printf debugging to inspect values at specific points in the kernel.
Apply conditional printing to focus on problematic values.
Implement runtime assertions in kernels to check invariants.
Validate data before and after kernel execution to catch anomalies.
Employ binary search to narrow down bug locations.
Disable code sections to isolate faulty logic.
Simplify complex kernels to minimal examples for easier debugging.
Compare kernel output with a reference implementation to verify correctness.
Develop incrementally by testing each component separately.
code_snippets:
def validate_and_launch(kernel, data, expected_min=None, expected_max=None):
    data_before = data.clone()
    kernel.launch(grid=[10,1,1], block=[256,1,1])(cute.from_dlpack(data))
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

def test_kernel_against_reference(kernel, A, B):
    C_kernel = torch.zeros(A.shape[0], B.shape[1], device='cuda', dtype=A.dtype)
    kernel.launch(grid=grid, block=block)(cute.from_dlpack(A), cute.from_dlpack(B), cute.from_dlpack(C_kernel))
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
constraints: Avoid debugging with large datasets; start small.
Ensure print statements are limited to prevent excessive output.
Always validate input and output data for NaN or Inf values.
Use assertions to enforce kernel assumptions.
Incremental development helps in identifying which change introduces a bug.
file_summaries.compressed_summary: Debugging GPU kernels in CuTe DSL involves a systematic approach due to the limited visibility of code running on a different processor. Key debugging techniques include print debugging, using assertions, isolating problems, reducing test cases, comparing with reference implementations, and incremental development. Print debugging involves using printf statements within kernels to inspect values at specific points, while conditional printing focuses on problematic values to avoid output spam. Assertions and validation check invariants and validate data before and after kernel execution to catch anomalies. Isolating problems can be achieved through binary search to narrow down bug locations, disabling code sections to isolate faulty logic, and simplifying complex kernels to minimal examples for easier debugging. Comparing kernel output with a reference implementation verifies correctness, and incremental development involves testing each component separately to ensure each part works before combining them. Constraints include starting with the simplest possible test to isolate bugs effectively, limiting print output to prevent excessive logs, and ensuring data validation to catch NaN or Inf values. Debugging tools such as cuda-memcheck, compute-sanitizer, and cuda-gdb can assist in detecting memory errors, race conditions, and performance bottlenecks. By following these strategies, developers can systematically identify and fix bugs in CuTe DSL kernels, ensuring efficient and correct GPU computations.

essential_patterns: Ensure all kernel parameters are properly annotated with CuTe types to avoid type errors.
Conduct diligent bounds checking and correct shared memory allocation to prevent memory errors.
Adhere to GPU constraints to resolve launch configuration errors, such as exceeding maximum threads per block.
Use syncthreads() to handle synchronization errors, ensuring all threads reach synchronization points.
Use supported Python constructs in JIT compilation to avoid compilation errors.
Implement print debugging and assertions to inspect values and validate data during kernel execution.
Isolate problems by simplifying kernels and using binary search to narrow down bug locations.
Compare kernel outputs with reference implementations to verify correctness.
Adopt incremental development by testing each component separately.
common_pitfalls: Missing annotations leading to type errors
Non-optimal block sizes or exceeding thread limits
Missing synchronization barriers causing race conditions
Syntax issues or unsupported constructs in JIT compilation
Excessive print output leading to log overflow
Neglecting data validation resulting in NaN or Inf values
compressed_overview: Debugging in CuTe DSL involves addressing a range of errors and employing systematic techniques to ensure reliable GPU kernel development. Developers must be vigilant about type annotations, memory allocation, and launch configurations to prevent common errors such as type mismatches, out-of-bounds access, and synchronization issues. Compilation errors often arise from syntax problems or unsupported constructs, which can be avoided by adhering to supported Python features. Debugging techniques include print debugging, assertions, and isolating problems through incremental development and test case reduction. Comparing outputs with reference implementations and using tools like cuda-memcheck and cuda-gdb can help identify and fix bugs. By following these strategies, developers can enhance the performance and correctness of their CuTe DSL kernels, ensuring efficient GPU computations.
